26

Jury Q&A drill

The questions that will actually be asked, with the answer to give. Click to open.

Q1Why four separate models instead of one? Isn't more data always better?

Neden tek bir model yerine dört ayrı model?

Because the panels do not share a solution. Their selected feature sets are almost disjoint — 137 selections cover only 106 distinct features, no feature is chosen in all four panels, and only four appear in three. Their optimal thresholds range from 0.280 to 0.810. And pooling would introduce leakage: panel identity correlates with the label because the base rates differ from 69% to 83%, so a pooled model would learn the panel prior instead of the biology.

We do use the extra data — just correctly. PAH and CFTR borrow GENEL rows as extra training rows, while still being evaluated only on their own rows.

Q2Your F1 is 0.94 on PAH. That's excellent, isn't it?

PAH'ta 0,94 F1 çok iyi değil mi?

No, and we say so in the report. The trivial classifier that labels every variant pathogenic already scores 0.909 on PAH, because 83% of PAH rows are pathogenic. Our lift is about +0.016 on the honest number. More importantly, PAH's nested ROC-AUC is 0.795 — the lowest in the project — and its balanced F1 is 0.735. The high F1 is mostly a base-rate effect. That is exactly why every table in our report prints the naive baseline next to the model score.

The panel we would actually point to is KANSER: baseline 0.817, model 0.933, a real lift of +0.116, with nested AUC 0.924.

Q3Where is your test set? You never split the data.

Test setiniz nerede? Veriyi hiç ayırmamışsınız.

We use nested cross-validation instead of a single fixed split, deliberately. On CFTR with 111 rows, a 20% holdout is 22 rows — a test estimate from 22 rows has enormous variance and costs us 22 training rows we cannot afford.

Nested CV gives the same guarantee without that cost: 5 outer folds × 2 repeats. Inside each outer fold, feature selection, base-model OOF, champion choice and the threshold are all determined on the outer-training rows only, then locked and scored exactly once on the untouched outer-test rows. Every row is used, and no row is ever scored by a pipeline that saw it. We report the mean and standard deviation over the 10 outer folds.

Q4Explain your stacking. And why did you keep it if it never won?

Stacking'i anlatın. Kazanmadıysa neden duruyor?

Two levels. Level 0 is five tuned base models — XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, ExtraTrees and L1 logistic regression — each producing out-of-fold probabilities. Level 1 is a logistic meta-learner trained on those columns. The critical detail: inside each meta-CV fold we first fit an isotonic calibrator per base column on that fold's training rows only, then fit the meta-learner on the calibrated values. So the meta OOF is honest end to end.

We evaluate two variants — trees-only and all-five — and both enter the champion pool. On all four panels the one-standard-error rule selected a single tuned booster instead. We report that negative result openly, and we still ship the ensemble in every bundle, so if a future run flips the decision the machinery is already there. Our reading is that with 111–2,931 rows and three highly correlated boosters, a meta-layer adds variance faster than it adds signal.

Q5How did you choose the final model? Just the best score?

Nihai modeli nasıl seçtiniz — sadece en yüksek skor mu?

No — taking the maximum of eight candidates measured on the same rows is selecting on noise. We use a one-standard-error rule. We score every candidate on ROC-AUC, bootstrap the out-of-fold rows 200 times to get a standard error, then take everything within one SE of the best and keep the simplest of those. Complexity order is single < mean < trees-stack < full stack.

In plain terms: an ensemble has to beat a single model by more than the measurement noise before we will ship it. It is Breiman's one-SE rule from CART, applied to model selection rather than tree pruning. We also found and fixed a flaw in it — at n=111 the marginal SE band was so wide that the simplest candidate always won by default, so the improved runner bootstraps the paired difference instead, which is a much tighter band.

Q6Why optimise ROC-AUC when the competition metric is F1?

Yarışma ölçütü F1 iken neden AUC optimize ettiniz?

Two reasons. First, the test set's class balance is unknown and the specification suggests it may be balanced, whereas our training data is 74% pathogenic. F1 is tied to the class prior; AUC ranks variants independently of it. Optimising F1 directly would have baked our training prior into the model.

Second, it separates two decisions that should be separate: which model ranks variants best, and where to cut. We choose the model on a threshold-free metric, then set the threshold afterwards from out-of-fold probabilities using the median of the per-fold optima. Doing both at once means the hyperparameter search overfits one specific operating point. F1 is still reported everywhere — it is just not the selector.

Q7Isn't borrowing rows from the GENEL panel data leakage?

GENEL panelinden satır ödünç almak sızdırma değil mi?

No, and here is the precise reason. We take only GENEL rows whose Variant_ID is not present in the target panel. Because those variants do not exist in the panel, they can never appear in any of that panel's cross-validation folds — so adding them to a training fold cannot leak a validation or test row. They go into training folds only; folds, threshold and every reported metric are computed on the panel's own rows.

We also verified the precondition: across the 578 variants that are shared between panels, the labels agree 100% of the time. The overlap is genuine duplication, not contradiction. And the augmentation is repeated inside the nested evaluation, so the honest score really is the augmented pipeline's score. It lifted CFTR's nested AUC from about 0.88 to 0.948.

Q8Why not SMOTE for the class imbalance?

Dengesizlik için neden SMOTE kullanmadınız?

SMOTE interpolates between nearest neighbours. In a 442-dimensional space where about 55% of the values are missing, that manufactures annotation profiles that cannot exist in reality — a variant that is simultaneously covered by one tool set and not by it. We chose to add real variants instead, borrowed leak-free from the GENEL panel. That raised PAH's benign training rows from 62 to 831 and CFTR's from 21 to 799 using genuine data.

Imbalance is also handled at the model level: scale_pos_weight with a searched multiplier from 0.5 to 6.0, CatBoost's balanced auto-weights, and class_weight for the other two.

Q9The column names are anonymised. How do you know what the features mean?

Kolon adları gizli. Özniteliklerin ne olduğunu nasıl biliyorsunuz?

We inferred the groups from their statistical signatures, and this is one of our claimed contributions. AL_1 to AL_26 are bounded in [0,1], strongly right-skewed, with medians around 10−4 — that is an allele-frequency signature. Other AL columns take only the values 0 and 1, so they are binary damaging flags; the rest are continuous risk scores. The EK columns are continuous over [−20, +11.93], consistent with conservation scores. CAT columns are low-cardinality strings, AA columns are single-letter amino-acid codes.

We then built the 91 derived features on those interpretations, and aggregated SHAP contributions at the group level so the explanation is clinically meaningful even without names. The group ranking we obtain — computational evidence, then population rarity, then biochemical context — matches the ACMG/AMP evidence hierarchy, which is independent confirmation that the interpretation is right.

Q10Is your model just detecting how much annotation a variant has?

Modeliniz aslında sadece anotasyon eksikliğini mi ölçüyor?

We measured exactly that, because it is the real risk. pct_missing alone reaches ROC-AUC 0.653 on GENEL, 0.769 on KANSER and 0.616 on CFTR. That is Grimm et al.'s circularity showing up in this dataset: rare pathogenic variants are sparsely annotated, common benign ones are well covered.

But the final models do not lean on it. Group-level SHAP puts annotation completeness at 6.9% on GENEL, 6.0% on KANSER and 0% on PAH and CFTR — those two panels select no missingness feature at all. Quantifying the shortcut and then showing it is not being exploited is one of the distinctive contributions of our work. And on PAH, pct_missing alone gives AUC 0.519, so the shortcut is not even available there.

Q11What does "one standard error" actually mean here? Show me the arithmetic.

"Bir standart hata" tam olarak ne demek?

Take a candidate's out-of-fold predictions. Resample the rows with replacement 200 times, recompute AUC each time, and take the standard deviation of those 200 values — that is the standard error, i.e. how much of the score is luck of the sample. Say the best candidate scores 0.947 with an SE of 0.012. The floor is 0.947 − 0.012 = 0.935. Every candidate at 0.935 or above is statistically indistinguishable from the best, so among those we keep the simplest one.

The improved version is tighter: instead of the best candidate's own SE, we bootstrap the difference between the best and each rival on the same resampled rows. Shared variance cancels, so the band narrows and a genuinely better ensemble can win rather than always losing to the simplicity tie-break.

Q12What happens if the real test set is balanced 50/50?

Gerçek test seti 1:1 çıkarsa ne olur?

We report that number explicitly — it is the balanced F1 row: 0.781 on GENEL, 0.852 on KANSER, 0.735 on PAH, 0.801 on CFTR. That is the worst case, computed by re-weighting positives and negatives to equal mass while deliberately keeping the threshold locked where it is.

Three things reduce that risk. Tuning and champion selection use ROC-AUC, which is balance-independent. The default threshold policy in the improved runner is minimax — it maximises the worse of F1-at-training-prior and F1-at-1:1, so it refuses to be terrible under either assumption. And because the isotonic calibrators are saved in the bundle, we can move the threshold to a new prior analytically, with a closed-form transform and no retraining.

Q13Why gradient boosting and not deep learning?

Neden derin öğrenme değil de gradyan artırma?

The data shape decides it: heterogeneous tabular columns, an average of 192 missing values per row, 111 to 2,931 rows, and hundreds of features. Boosted trees handle missing values natively by learning a default split direction, capture non-monotonic interactions, need no scaling, and support TreeSHAP explanation. The closest published work on tabular variant annotation converges on the same family — Jain et al. and DiagAI both land on XGBoost.

Deep tabular models like TabNet or FT-Transformer would overfit at 111–388 rows and are much harder to explain, which is scored here. Protein language models like AlphaMissense and ESM1b are stronger in the literature but need the protein sequence and residue position, and both are hidden in this dataset — so they are not an option, not a rejected preference.

Q14Explain null-importance feature selection to someone who hasn't heard of it.

Null-importance seçimini anlatın.

With 442 features and as few as 111 rows, some features will look predictive purely by chance. Null-importance asks each feature: how much importance do you earn from the real labels, compared with the importance you earn from randomly shuffled labels?

We fit LightGBM five times on the real labels and average the gain importance. Then we fit it 40–50 times on shuffled labels, which gives each feature its own null distribution — its personal noise ceiling. A feature is kept if its real gain exceeds the 95th percentile of its own null distribution. We add one safeguard: a top-K floor, K = n_rows/12 clipped to [10, 50], which is strictly inclusive and protects against the gate's instability as the candidate pool changes. It reduced 442 features to 52, 35, 37 and 13 per panel.

Q15What did the Orange Data Mining work actually contribute?

Orange çalışması ne kattı?

It produced our most useful counter-intuitive finding. Using Orange's Rank widget we compared three rankings — Information Gain, ANOVA F and ReliefF — and t-SNE per panel. Two results: KANSER separates best and GENEL worst; and many GENEL AL features have negative ReliefF, meaning they make a variant's nearest neighbours harder to classify.

We then tested it properly. Adding KANSER's four highest Information-Gain features reduced held-out F1 from 0.9326 to 0.9314 — they were redundant with signal already present. Removing negative-ReliefF features instead raised held-out F1 from 0.891 to 0.911 with 22 features instead of 36. So we reimplemented all three rankings inside the pipeline and built a hybrid selector where ReliefF acts as a second gate on top of null-importance. Information Gain measures global predictiveness; ReliefF measures local separability. They are not interchangeable.

Q16If the hybrid selector was better, why did you ship the plain one?

Hibrit seçici daha iyiyse neden varsayılan yapmadınız?

Because it was only better on one panel by more than noise. The pattern across the held-out A/B is consistent — pruning helps or is neutral everywhere, adding hurts or is neutral everywhere — but only KANSER's margin (+0.020) exceeds single-split variability. GENEL's +0.002 and PAH's +0.004 are inside the noise band.

Our acceptance rule is that a method enters the mainline only if it wins on an independent held-out test or a multi-seed trial. Trusting a +0.002 improvement measured once is precisely the mistake that produces a model which looks good in development and fails on the jury's test set. We chose to give up a little expected score for robustness against an unknown test distribution, and we state that trade-off in the report.

Q17Your thresholds range from 0.28 to 0.81. Isn't that arbitrary?

Eşikleriniz 0,28 ile 0,81 arasında — keyfi değil mi?

They are derived, not chosen. For each fold we scan thresholds from 0.05 to 0.95 in steps of 0.005 and take that fold's F1-optimum; the shipped value is the median across folds, which prevents one lucky fold from dictating the operating point — a pooled scan once gave 0.135 on CFTR, which is clearly an artefact.

The spread reflects panel character and is interpretable. GENEL and PAH separate weakly, so a low threshold protects sensitivity. CFTR's probabilities separate sharply, so the best trade-off sits at 0.810. The bias toward sensitivity is a clinical choice: a false negative can mean a missed diagnosis, while a false positive means an extra confirmatory test. Sensitivity stays between 0.955 and 0.994 on all four panels, and we report the cost of that in the balanced-F1 row.

Q18How do we know you didn't overfit while developing this?

Geliştirme sırasında aşırı uyum yapmadığınızı nasıl bilelim?

We measure it and print it. Every table shows optimism_gap = OOF F1 minus nested F1, and it stays between +0.005 and +0.034. The pattern is exactly what theory predicts — smallest on the 2,931-row panel, largest on the 111-row one. If we were overfitting badly, that gap would be large and would not track sample size.

Structurally: feature selection is re-run inside every outer fold; the threshold is a fold median; the champion is chosen by a one-SE rule that prefers simplicity; hyperparameter search uses fold-seed jitter and a threshold-free objective; tree depth is capped on small panels. And our sweep script has an explicit overfitting audit that eliminates configurations with a gap above 0.040, or whose champion is unstable across outer folds — PAH producing four different winners across ten folds is exactly the signature that test catches.

The one thing we do not do is re-tune hyperparameters inside each outer fold, for runtime reasons. That leaves a small residual optimism, and we state it in the report rather than hiding it.

Q19Which panel is your weakest result, and what would you do about it?

En zayıf paneliniz hangisi, ne yapardınız?

PAH, without question. Nested AUC 0.795, balanced F1 0.735, and 39 of its 62 benign variants are false positives. We understand why: PAH has no missingness shortcut (pct_missing alone gives AUC 0.519 there), so the model depends purely on in-silico scores, and those scores are weak at separating PAH's benign variants. SHAP confirms it — 42.5% of PAH's decision comes from in-silico scores and only 11% from conservation.

What we already did: cross-panel augmentation raised its benign training rows from 62 to 831, and we widened the class-weight search so the model could reach the equal-weight regime. What we would do next: keep sweeping partial augmentation fractions, use the minimax threshold policy which explicitly protects the balanced case, and look for PAH-specific features in the continuous predictor profile rather than the binary flags. §17 sets that out in full, with the commands and the target numbers.

Q20Can this run in a real clinical setting?

Bu gerçek bir klinik ortamda çalışabilir mi?

Training is a one-off, roughly four and a half hours on a Colab GPU for the three large panels at full budget. Inference is effectively instant: all 2,931 GENEL rows in 0.67 seconds, which is 0.23 ms per variant, and a single variant end-to-end — loading the bundle and building features included — in 65 to 124 milliseconds, dropping below a millisecond if the bundle stays in memory. Peak memory is 305 MB and the champion model itself is under half a megabyte.

We also verified the whole pipeline CPU-only on a laptop-class Ryzen 7 with the same feature selection result, so no GPU is required. Everything is seeded at 42, and each run logs its exact command, library versions, hardware and git commit.

Q21Why did you merge "Likely Pathogenic" into "Pathogenic"?

Neden "Likely Pathogenic"i "Pathogenic" ile birleştirdiniz?

The competition defines the binary task that way, following ACMG/AMP: Pathogenic plus Likely Pathogenic become class 1, Benign plus Likely Benign become class 0, and there are no VUS records in the data. We name the limitation explicitly in the report — a "Likely" record carries weaker evidence, so the model learns two confidence levels as a single class. We accept it because splitting them would shrink the already tiny benign class further; PAH has only 62 benign rows and CFTR only 21.

Q22What is the single most original thing in this project?

Projenin en özgün yanı nedir?

Five things, in the order we would rank them:

1. Leak-free cross-panel augmentation — solving a minority-class problem with real borrowed data instead of synthetic oversampling, with the 100% label-agreement measurement that makes it defensible. 2. Deriving feature-group semantics from statistical signatures alone, with no column names, and then aggregating SHAP at that group level and mapping it to ACMG evidence codes. 3. The ReliefF-gated hybrid selector — adding a local-separability gate on top of a global gain test, with the ablation showing that adding high-Information-Gain features hurts while pruning helps. 4. A decision architecture built for distribution shift — AUC objective, one-SE simplicity preference, fold-median threshold, and stored calibrators that let the threshold move to a new class prior without retraining. 5. Measuring and bounding the shortcut signal instead of ignoring it — naming the circularity, quantifying it, and showing SHAP keeps it under 7%.

Q23What would you do differently with more time?

Daha fazla zamanınız olsa neyi farklı yapardınız?

Four concrete things, all already scaffolded in the repo. Re-tune hyperparameters inside each outer fold (NESTED_RETUNE=1) to remove the last residual optimism from the honest number. Finish the full configuration sweep in run_best_search.py, especially partial augmentation fractions on KANSER, which the reference run never tried. Give the meta-learner genuinely different input views rather than different model families, since the boosters are too correlated to combine — the diverse-view stack in the improved runner is the first step. And find PAH-specific signal, because PAH is where the headroom is.

Q24How is your solution reproducible?

Çözümünüz nasıl tekrarlanabilir?

Seed 42 everywhere. The reference runner is auto-generated from the notebook that produced the reported numbers, so there is no drift between what we ran and what we report. Every run writes a log with its date, exact command, library versions, CPU/RAM/GPU, git commit and every active environment variable, and finishes with a duration and a success or traceback footer.

On the modelling side, training and inference call the same feature-construction function, and the bundle stores the selected feature list, the categorical vocabulary and the threshold — so a train/serve mismatch is structurally impossible rather than merely tested for. We also verified the pipeline CPU-only on a different machine and reproduced the same feature selection.

Q25How does this work in real life — clinical integration, innovation and commercial potential?

Gerçek hayatta nasıl kullanılır — klinik entegrasyon, yenilikçilik ve girişimcilik potansiyeli?

Where it sits in the workflow. A diagnostic genetics lab already produces, for every variant it sequences, exactly the kind of annotation table this model consumes: population frequencies, in-silico predictor scores, conservation metrics, the amino-acid change. Our model plugs in immediately after that annotation step and before human curation, and it does one job — triage. It ranks and pre-classifies the variant list so that the curator's time goes to the cases that need judgement rather than to the obvious ones. It is decision support, never an autonomous diagnosis.

Why the architecture is already clinically shaped. This is the part we would emphasise: labs do not order "generic sequencing", they run panels — a hereditary cancer panel, a cystic fibrosis panel, a phenylketonuria panel. Our four independent per-panel models mirror exactly how the clinic is organised. A lab that only runs CF testing deploys the CFTR bundle and nothing else. The architectural decision we made for statistical reasons turns out to be the natural deployment and packaging unit too.

What makes it deployable today. Inference is 0.23 ms per variant in batch and 65–124 ms for a single variant end to end; peak memory is 305 MB; the champion model is under half a megabyte; and we verified the whole pipeline CPU-only, so no GPU is required. It runs on a laptop or a small on-premises server. That last point matters more than the speed: genomic data is among the most sensitive data a hospital holds, and our solution makes zero external calls — no ClinVar query, no cloud API, no external database. The data never leaves the institution. For a hospital IT and ethics committee, that is often the difference between a pilot and a refusal.

Three things a curator actually gets. First, a calibrated probability, not just a label — isotonic calibration means 0.8 really corresponds to roughly 80% of such variants being pathogenic, so the number can be reasoned about. Second, a group-level explanation expressed in the vocabulary they already use: our SHAP groups map onto ACMG/AMP evidence codes — computational evidence (PP3/BP4), population rarity (PM2/BA1), biochemical context (PP2/BP1). The output speaks the curator's language rather than asking them to learn ours. Third, a configurable operating point: because the calibrators are stored in the bundle, a lab can move the threshold to its own disease prevalence with a closed-form transform and no retraining.

The concrete product: a three-band triage. Our error analysis points straight at the design. On KANSER, only 6 of 27 false positives sit near the threshold and none of the 12 false negatives do — errors are either at the boundary or confidently wrong, not spread evenly. So the useful deployment is not one threshold but two: auto-accept above a high-confidence cut, auto-reject below a low one, and route the middle band to a human. That converts our calibrated probabilities into measurable saved curator hours, which is the number a lab director will actually buy on.

What is genuinely innovative here. Four things, and they are engineering contributions rather than a new architecture: leak-free cross-panel augmentation that solves a minority-class problem with real borrowed data instead of synthetic oversampling; deriving feature-group semantics from statistical signatures alone, with no column names, and mapping them to clinical evidence codes; a ReliefF-gated selector that adds a local-separability test on top of a global importance test; and a decision layer explicitly built for distribution shift — AUC-driven selection, a one-standard-error simplicity rule, fold-median thresholds and stored calibrators. All four transfer to any small-cohort clinical tabular problem, not just this one.

Commercial shape. Realistically it is a module, not a standalone product: a component inside an existing clinical genomics pipeline or LIMS, licensed on-premises to diagnostic laboratories, with per-panel model packs as the unit of sale and periodic retraining as the recurring service. Cost of goods is close to zero — training is a one-off few hours, inference is negligible, and because every feature is derived from the lab's own annotation output we carry no external data licensing, which several commercial in-silico predictors do.

And what would have to happen first — we would say this unprompted. Three honest gates. (1) Scale and validation: 3,802 variants from a competition dataset is a proof of concept, not clinical evidence; it needs prospective validation on each deploying lab's own cohort. (2) Regulatory: as software in a diagnostic pathway it falls under medical-device software rules — TİTCK in Türkiye, IVDR/CE-IVD in the EU — which requires a quality system, clinical performance evidence and an audit trail, all of which is why we log every run with its versions, hardware, seed and git commit. (3) The VUS problem: our training data contains no variants of uncertain significance, yet VUS is precisely where clinical labs lose the most time and where the commercial value really sits. Extending to a three-class or explicit "uncertain" output is the honest next step, and our calibrated probabilities plus the middle-band design are the right foundation for it.

Last thing before you walk in

If you get one sentence, make it this: "Four independent per-panel models, selected on AUC with a one-standard-error simplicity rule, and reported with a leak-free nested-CV score next to the naive baseline — mean honest F1 0.917, with an optimism gap never above 0.034." Everything else in this document is elaboration on that sentence.
